questions.q: In standard clinical clerkship history taking, which section immediately follows the Presenting Complaint (PC)?
questions.explain: The History of Presenting Complaint (HPC) immediately follows the Presenting Complaint to chronologically detail the onset, progression, severity, and associated symptoms of the main problem.

open.q: Which section of a standard medical clerking immediately follows the Presenting Complaint?

questions.q: In the SOCRATES mnemonic used to characterize pain during history taking, what does the letter 'R' represent?
questions.explain: SOCRATES stands for Site, Onset, Character, Radiation, Associations, Time course, Exacerbating/relieving factors, and Severity.

open.q: What do the eight letters of the SOCRATES mnemonic stand for when analyzing a patient's pain?
accept: Site, Onset, Character, Radiation, Associations, Time course, Exacerbating and relieving factors, Severity
Site Onset Character Radiation Associations Time Exacerbating Severity

questions.q: Which anatomical site is most reliable for inspecting subtle clinical jaundice in natural daylight?
options: The sclerae, examined in natural daylight
questions.explain: Elastin-rich tissues such as the sclera (bulbar conjunctiva) have a high affinity for bilirubin, making mild hyperbilirubinaemia (>35-50 micromol/L) earliest and best detected under natural daylight.

open.q: Where on the body is mild jaundice earliest and most reliably detected on physical examination?

questions.q: Which anatomical site should be inspected to differentiate central cyanosis from peripheral cyanosis?
questions.explain: Central cyanosis reflects systemic arterial hypoxaemia and affects warm, well-perfused mucosae such as the tongue and sublingual mucosa, whereas peripheral cyanosis affects cold extremities alone.

open.q: Which mucosal site is examined to confirm central cyanosis rather than peripheral cyanosis?

questions.q: Schamroth's window test is performed during physical examination to detect which clinical sign?
options: Loss of the normal diamond-shaped gap between the fingers
questions.explain: Apposing the dorsal surfaces of corresponding fingers normally leaves a small diamond-shaped window at the nail base; obliteration of this space confirms early finger clubbing.

open.q: What clinical sign is confirmed by obliteration of the diamond-shaped gap during Schamroth's window test?

questions.q: At what angle should a patient's upper body be inclined on the examination couch to accurately assess the Jugular Venous Pressure (JVP)?
questions.explain: Positioning the patient at 45 degrees places the upper meniscus of the internal jugular venous column just above the clavicle in normal individuals, allowing vertical measurement above the sternal angle.

open.q: At what degree of trunk inclination is the patient positioned to measure the Jugular Venous Pressure?

questions.q: What is the anatomical surface landmark for the normal cardiac apex beat in an adult?
options: Left 4th intercostal space in the anterior axillary line
Left 2nd intercostal space at the sternal border
Left 5th intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line
Right 5th intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line
questions.explain: The normal apex beat is the lowest and outermost point of definite cardiac impulse, located in the left 5th intercostal space at or medial to the mid-clavicular line.

open.q: State the normal anatomical surface location of the cardiac apex beat in an adult.
accept: Left 5th intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line
Left fifth intercostal space midclavicular line

questions.q: During precordial auscultation, a clinician hears a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumbling murmur localized at the apex. Which manoeuvre and stethoscope part best accentuate this murmur?
options: Diaphragm at the right second intercostal space with the patient leaning forward
Bell at the left lower sternal edge during inspiration
Diaphragm at the apex during deep inspiration
Bell lightly at the apex with the patient in the left lateral position
questions.explain: Low-pitched murmurs like mitral stenosis are best heard using the stethoscope bell lightly applied over the apex while the patient lies in the left lateral position, bringing the left ventricle closer to the chest wall.

open.q: Which patient position and stethoscope chestpiece best accentuate the low-pitched mid-diastolic murmur of mitral stenosis?
accept: Left lateral position using the bell
Left lateral decubitus with the bell
Bell of stethoscope in left lateral position

questions.q: Which percussion note is typically elicited over a large free-flowing pleural effusion during chest examination?
questions.explain: Fluid in the pleural cavity dampens chest wall vibrations markedly, producing a characteristic flat, stony dull percussion note accompanied by absent breath sounds and reduced vocal fremitus.

open.q: What characteristic percussion note is heard over a large pleural effusion?

questions.q: A 36-year-old man presents with acute pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea. Examination of the right hemithorax reveals reduced chest expansion, tracheal deviation to the left, hyper-resonant percussion, and absent breath sounds. What is the underlying mechanical abnormality?
options: Right lower-lobe consolidation with air bronchograms
Right main bronchus obstruction causing uncomplicated collapse
questions.explain: Air trapped under pressure in the right pleural space causes hyper-resonance, absent breath sounds, and pushes the mediastinum and trachea away toward the contralateral (left) side.

open.q: Which pleural condition produces hyper-resonant percussion, absent breath sounds, and tracheal deviation away from the affected side?

questions.q: What is the proper sequence of the four cardinal steps in routine physical examination of the thorax?
questions.explain: In cardiovascular and respiratory examinations, the standard sequence is Inspection, Palpation, Percussion, and Auscultation (unlike the abdomen, where auscultation precedes percussion and palpation).

open.q: List the four standard physical examination steps in their proper order for respiratory examination.

questions.q: Why is abdominal auscultation performed before percussion and palpation during a gastrointestinal physical examination?
options: To avoid manipulating the abdomen before listening for bowel sounds
Because percussion makes the liver produce bowel sounds
Because auscultation is only possible before the patient lies supine
To prevent the examiner's hands from becoming cold
questions.explain: Mechanical manipulation of the abdominal wall during palpation or percussion stimulates bowel peristalsis, which can mask true hypoactive or absent bowel sounds.

open.q: Why must abdominal auscultation precede palpation and percussion during abdominal examination?
accept: Palpation and percussion can alter bowel sounds and stimulate peristalsis
To avoid artificially stimulating bowel motility

questions.q: From which abdominal quadrant should palpation for splenomegaly begin in a patient with suspected massive splenomegaly?
questions.explain: An enlarged spleen grows inferomedially from beneath the left costal margin toward the right iliac fossa; starting in the right iliac fossa prevents missing the inferior edge of a massive spleen.

open.q: In which abdominal region should palpation for splenomegaly begin so a massively enlarged spleen is not missed?

questions.q: During abdominal examination, a clinician percusses from the midline umbilicus toward the left flank, notes dullness, keeps the pleximeter finger stationary, and rolls the patient onto their right side for 30 seconds before re-percussing. Which clinical sign is being elicited?
questions.explain: Shifting dullness detects moderate free intraperitoneal fluid (ascites, typically >500-1000 mL) as dependent fluid gravitates to the right flank and air-filled bowel loops float upward, turning the left flank resonant.

open.q: Name the bedside percussion test used to confirm moderate ascites by rolling the patient onto one side and re-percussing the flank.

questions.q: How is a positive Murphy's sign elicited during right upper quadrant palpation?
options: Rebound tenderness in the right iliac fossa upon sudden release of pressure
Pain in the right iliac fossa when pressing the left iliac fossa
Inspiratory arrest due to sharp pain when palpating beneath the right costal margin
Tenderness over the renal angle on gentle fist percussion
questions.explain: In acute cholecystitis, deep inspiration pushes the inflamed gallbladder downward against the examiner's fingers under the right costal margin, causing sudden pain and inspiratory arrest.

open.q: Describe what constitutes a positive Murphy's sign on abdominal palpation.
accept: Sudden pain and inspiratory arrest when palpating the right subcostal area during deep inspiration
Inspiratory arrest on right subcostal palpation
Catching of breath from pain on palpating right hypochondrium

questions.q: Which three clinical parameters are scored in the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)?
options: Pupillary size, corneal reflex, and plantar response
Respiratory rate, blood pressure, and heart rate
Orientation, short-term memory, and speech fluency
Eye opening, verbal response, and motor response
questions.explain: The Glasgow Coma Scale evaluates consciousness across Eye opening (1-4), Verbal response (1-5), and Motor response (1-6), yielding a total score ranging from 3 to 15.

open.q: Name the three behavioral responses evaluated in the Glasgow Coma Scale.
accept: Eye opening, verbal response, and motor response

questions.q: Which spinal nerve root is primarily tested when eliciting the ankle jerk (Achilles tendon reflex)?
questions.explain: The Achilles tendon reflex tests the S1 (and S2) nerve root via the tibial nerve, whereas the knee jerk tests L3-L4.

open.q: Which primary spinal nerve root is evaluated by the ankle (Achilles) deep tendon reflex?

questions.q: A 62-year-old man presents with left-sided facial drooping. Examination shows inability to close the left eye, loss of left forehead wrinkling, and drooping of the left corner of the mouth. Where is the anatomical lesion located?
options: Right cerebral cortex above the facial nucleus
Left facial nucleus or peripheral facial nerve
Right facial nerve after it exits the stylomastoid foramen
questions.explain: Because the upper face receives bilateral cortical innervation, paralysis involving both the forehead and lower face indicates an ipsilateral lower motor neuron lesion of cranial nerve VII (e.g., Bell's palsy).

open.q: How does a lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy differ clinically from an upper motor neuron facial palsy on examination of the forehead?
accept: Lower motor neuron palsy involves the forehead whereas upper motor neuron palsy spares the forehead
Forehead wrinkling is lost in LMN palsy and spared in UMN palsy
LMN affects upper and lower face while UMN spares the upper face

questions.q: What constitutes an abnormal Babinski (extensor plantar) response in an adult?
options: Great-toe dorsiflexion with fanning of other toes
No toe movement after lateral sole stimulation
questions.explain: Stroking the lateral border of the sole normally causes plantar flexion of the toes; dorsiflexion (upgoing) of the big toe with fanning of the lateral toes indicates an upper motor neuron (corticospinal tract) lesion.

open.q: Describe a positive Babinski sign and state what neurological pathway lesion it indicates in an adult.
accept: Upgoing big toe with fanning of other toes indicating an upper motor neuron lesion
Dorsiflexion of the hallux indicating corticospinal tract lesion
Extensor plantar response due to UMN lesion

questions.q: Which sign of meningeal irritation is elicited by flexing the patient's hip and knee to 90 degrees and then attempting to passively extend the knee, resulting in pain and hamstring spasm?
questions.explain: Kernig's sign tests meningeal irritation by stretching inflamed lumbar nerve roots when extending the knee from a 90-degree flexed hip position.

open.q: Name the meningeal irritation sign characterized by pain and resistance upon extending the knee while the hip is flexed at 90 degrees.

questions.q: During Romberg's test, a patient stands steadily with feet together and eyes open, but sways markedly and nearly falls as soon as they close their eyes. Which neurological pathway is defective?
options: Dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway or its peripheral afferents
questions.explain: A positive Romberg's sign indicates sensory ataxia due to impaired joint position sense (proprioception) in the dorsal columns or peripheral nerves; cerebellar ataxia causes unsteadiness even with eyes open.

open.q: What does a positive Romberg's test indicate about the underlying cause of a patient's ataxia?
accept: Sensory ataxia due to proprioceptive loss

questions.q: What error in blood pressure measurement occurs if a sphygmomanometer cuff bladder is too narrow or too short for an obese patient's upper arm?
options: An isolated fall in diastolic pressure
questions.explain: An undersized cuff requires excessive inflation pressure to compress the brachial artery beneath it, producing spuriously elevated blood pressure readings ('cuff hypertension').

open.q: How does using an undersized sphygmomanometer cuff affect measured blood pressure values?
accept: Produces falsely high blood pressure readings

questions.q: Which Korotkoff sound phase corresponds to the standard auscultatory diastolic blood pressure in resting adults?
options: Phase I, first clear tapping sound
questions.explain: Korotkoff Phase I marks systolic blood pressure, while Phase V (complete disappearance of sounds) marks diastolic blood pressure in most adults (Phase IV muffling is used when sounds persist to zero, as in pregnancy or aortic regurgitation).

open.q: Which Korotkoff phase marks the diastolic blood pressure in routine adult sphygmomanometry?

questions.q: A 48-year-old woman with exertional syncope has a slow-rising, low-amplitude carotid pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus) and an ejection systolic murmur radiating to both carotids. Which valvular lesion best explains these examination findings?
questions.explain: Fixed left ventricular outflow obstruction in severe aortic stenosis prolongs ventricular ejection, producing a slow-rising, low-volume pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus) and a crescendo-decrescendo murmur radiating to the carotids.

open.q: Which valvular heart lesion produces a slow-rising, low-volume pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus) and an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the neck?

questions.q: Where should the clinician stand when palpating the cervical lymph nodes and thyroid gland?
options: Behind the seated patient with both hands placed gently around the neck
In front of the supine patient using one thumb
At the foot of the bed while the patient hyperextends the neck
Directly to the left of the standing patient
questions.explain: Palpating the neck from behind a seated patient with the neck slightly flexed relaxes the sternocleidomastoid muscles and allows simultaneous bimanual comparison of cervical lymph node chains and thyroid lobes.

open.q: From which position relative to the seated patient are the cervical lymph nodes and thyroid gland palpated?

questions.q: Which screening acronym is widely used during social history taking to screen a patient for alcohol misuse or dependence?
questions.explain: The CAGE questionnaire asks four questions: Have you ever felt you should Cut down, been Annoyed by criticism of your drinking, felt Guilty about drinking, or needed an Eye-opener drink first thing in the morning?

open.q: What do the four letters of the CAGE alcohol screening questionnaire stand for?

questions.q: Which clinical sign on examination of the hands and nails is classically associated with severe chronic iron deficiency anaemia?
questions.explain: Koilonychia (thin, brittle, concave spoon-shaped nails) is a classic peripheral trophic sign of long-standing iron deficiency anaemia.

open.q: What is the clinical term for concave, spoon-shaped fingernails seen in chronic iron deficiency anaemia?

questions.q: A 55-year-old man with chronic alcohol use presents with abdominal distension, spider naevi, palmar erythema, and prominent tortuous veins radiating outward from the umbilicus. What is this abdominal wall sign called and what does it signify?
questions.explain: Caput medusae represents dilated, tortuous paraumbilical collateral veins radiating away from the umbilicus due to elevated portal venous pressure in cirrhosis.

open.q: What is the clinical name for dilated tortuous veins radiating outward from the umbilicus in portal hypertension?

questions.q: Which pair of cranial nerves mediates the afferent and efferent limbs of the corneal blink reflex?
options: Afferent: Trigeminal nerve (CN V1); Efferent: Facial nerve (CN VII)
Afferent: Optic nerve (CN II); Efferent: Oculomotor nerve (CN III)
Afferent: Facial nerve (CN VII); Efferent: Trigeminal nerve (CN V)
Afferent: Oculomotor nerve (CN III); Efferent: Abducens nerve (CN VI)
questions.explain: Lightly touching the cornea stimulates sensory fibres of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1), triggering bilateral blinking via motor fibres of the facial nerve (CN VII) to orbicularis oculi.

open.q: Name the cranial nerves responsible for the afferent sensory limb and efferent motor limb of the corneal reflex.
accept: Afferent CN V1 and efferent CN VII

questions.q: Which auscultatory finding is produced by the sudden opening of collapsed small airways and alveoli during inspiration, commonly heard in pulmonary fibrosis or left ventricular failure?
questions.explain: Crackles (crepitations) are discontinuous, non-musical popping sounds heard predominantly during inspiration when deflated small airways snap open or air bubbles through alveolar fluid.

open.q: What discontinuous, non-musical lung sounds are heard on auscultation when collapsed alveoli snap open or fluid is present in small airways?
